core.text: Which tense of the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do) goes inside an *ut*, *nē*, *cum* or question clause depends on the main verb. That pairing is **the sequence of tenses (a present main verb takes the present subjunctive, a past one the imperfect)**: *imperat ut veniās* (he orders you to come) but *imperāvit ut venīrēs* (he ordered you to come). Latin name: *consecutio temporum*.
English shifts too: he says he *is* coming; he said he *was* coming. The tense of the report follows the tense of the main verb.

Main verb present or future → present subjunctive; main verb imperfect, perfect or pluperfect → imperfect subjunctive. The same rule covers purpose, result, indirect command, cum clauses and indirect questions.

invented.la: Rogat ut maneam. — Rogāvit ut manērem.
invented.en: He asks me to stay. — He asked me to stay.

core.text: The imperfect subjunctive is not 'past meaning' but 'past setting': in *vēnit ut vidēret* the seeing is still ahead from his point of view. Choose the tense by the main verb, then translate the clause naturally ('to see', 'to stay').

more.text: The learner's notes list five dependent uses and shift each one: *imperō / imperābō ut veniās* but *imperāvī ut venīrēs*; *veniō ut doceam* but *vēnī ut docērem*; *ita clāmō ut proximōs suscitem* but *clāmāvī ut suscitārem*; *bibō cum sitiam* (I drink because I am thirsty) but *bibēbam cum sitīrem*; *nesciō quid videam* but *nesciēbam quid vidērem*.

Two more tenses fill in 'already finished': after a present main verb the perfect subjunctive (Week 10: *nesciō quid fēcerit*, I don't know what he did), after a past main verb the pluperfect subjunctive (Week 12: *nesciēbam quid fēcisset*). So each main-verb group has a 'same time' tense and a 'before' tense.

In a present-tense story (the historic present) a writer may still use the imperfect: *rogat ut manēret*; the story is past even if the verb is present. Ørberg's chapter 28 drills the pair with *monet ut pāreat* / *monēbat, monuit ut pārēret*; chapter 29 sets *tempus praesēns* against *tempus praeteritum* for purpose and result alike.
